Mahfuz, Asma and Irteza — thank you for the opportunity to put this together. Everything in it comes from the records and from one MLS® pull run this week: every condominium townhouse sold within the search radius since June, every one for sale now, and the city and district figures behind them. We have not walked through yet, so the number here is an estimate from the records and from the photographs of the home as it was listed in 2019 — which, we understand, is how it still stands; the walkthrough turns it into a pricing strategy. One thing shapes the document: in this part of Scarborough, condominium townhouses are being bought on two numbers together, the price and the monthly fee, and the home that sells is the one that reads as the best value on both. Our reading of the evidence is stated once, at the end, and labelled as ours.

Section 01 · The property

A three-bedroom multi-level townhouse in the Cliffcrest enclave at Kingston and McCowan, with hardwood, stone and a garden walk-out — kept as it was finished.

Townhouse 43 is a 1,292 sq ft multi-level unit in York Condominium Corporation 392, a 1977 complex of brick townhouses set back from Kingston Road east of McCowan. Three bedrooms, a four-piece and two two-piece baths, a built-in garage with a second space on the drive, ensuite laundry, and a finished lower level that walks out to a fenced west-facing garden. The home was renovated before the current owners bought it in 2019 — Canadian maple hardwood and Carrara stone floors, an updated kitchen with under-cabinet lighting, two Fujitsu ductless heat pumps — and has been kept in that condition since. The monthly fee is $600 and includes water, building insurance, common elements and parking.

Sale price ($000s) · Cliffcrest, Scarborough Village, Eglinton East and Birchcliffe-Cliffside · June – September 2026

SYNERGY's extract from MLS®, June 1 – September 30, 2026. Nine condominium townhouse sales between 1,100 and 1,500 sq ft in the four communities; stacked units and the two sales over $1.2M excluded. The three complexes with fees above $730 a month sold at $440,000–$460,000; the five with fees under $650 sold at $550,000–$663,000.

Three things to hold at once. Condominium townhouses across Toronto are selling far less often than a year ago — a third fewer in September — and at a median 6% lower, with August the weakest month of the year. Buyers are still paying 98% of the asking price when the asking price is right, which means the price is what moves, not the discount. And in this pocket the monthly fee is read as hard as the price: the chart above puts nine sales in a line, and the fee predicts the sale price almost as well as the size does.

Board statistics stop at the district line and E08 reported two condominium townhouse sales last month, so we pull our own MLS® data on the 1st of each month — every sale in the five regions — before the board publishes. During your listing that means we see a shift in this pocket and respond to it while other agents are waiting for the report.

Section 05 · What each sale tells us

One sale sets the ceiling for the complex and one the floor for the form — and the gap between them is almost entirely renovation.

3100 Kingston Rd #14 · your complex

$645,000

Sold August 6 · 96% of final list · 110 days across four listings

The ceiling. A 1,464 sq ft three-storey end unit, four bedrooms and four baths, with "over $200,000" of work — kitchen, all baths in 2025, deck, windows and roof — a wood-burning fireplace and a $541 fee. It opened at $831,000 in April, was relisted twice, and sold in August at $645,000. Two lessons: the most renovated townhouse in the complex could not clear $650,000 this year, and asking $831,000 for it cost the seller four months. Against TH 43 it has 172 more square feet, an extra bedroom and bath, and a renovation ten years newer.

3430 Kingston Rd #4 · Scarborough Village

$550,000

Sold June 18 · 92% of final list · 87 days

The floor for the form. The same multi-level plan at the same size — 1,283 sq ft, three bedrooms, garage and drive — in a 1970s complex a kilometre east, with a $635 fee. Hardwood on the upper levels, a solid-wood kitchen, a finished basement; staged and vacant. It asked $699,000, cut three times, and sold at $550,000. TH 43 is the same house in a better-regarded complex, with the lower fee, the stone and maple floors and the renovated kitchen the Scarborough Village unit did not have — and a third bath.

The pattern

Both sales ran the same course: an ambitious opening price, three months, a sale at 85–92% of the original ask. 3430 Kingston #4 is the same home as yours in a lesser complex — $550,000. 3100 Kingston #14 is a bigger, fully renovated unit in your complex — $645,000. TH 43 sits between them: the complex and the finishes lift it off the floor, and the size and the age of the renovation keep it under the ceiling. The actives in Section 07 say where in between.

The two sales bracket the home. Built up from the Scarborough Village twin, the complex, the floors, the kitchen, the third bath and the lower fee carry TH 43 to about $585,000. Built down from the renovated end unit in your own complex, the size, the extra rooms and the age of the renovation take it to the mid-$540,000s — but that sale, after four months and four listings, was a weak one. The unit still for sale in the complex, HS47, says the ceiling plainly: 22 square feet bigger than yours and move-in ready, it has found no buyer at $705,000 or, so far, at $659,000. The midpoint of $585,000 reconciles the three, and the 2019 purchase price carried forward at the city's condominium-townhouse index lands within a few thousand dollars of it. At $453 per square foot it sits above the Scarborough Village sale's $429 — the better complex and finishes — and above #14's $441, which a smaller unit should carry.

This estimate is built from the records and from the 2019 photographs. A walkthrough — the kitchen and baths as they stand today, the floors, the lower level and the walk-out, the heat pumps, and anything the seven years since have left — is what turns it into a pricing strategy. Until then, treat it as a well-supported starting point rather than a number to list at.

Section 07 · Who you would be competing with

Four condominium townhouses are for sale in the radius. None has sold in between 40 and 293 days, and the one in your complex has been asking more than $659,000 since January.

A buyer looking at TH 43 will have these four open in other tabs. The fourth is HS47 in your own complex: 1,314 sq ft, three bedrooms, two baths, a wood fireplace and a finished walk-out, listed in January at $741,000 after a 2025 attempt at $778,000, reduced to $705,000 in June and to $659,000 in October. Ten months without a buyer in the same complex is the single most useful fact in this document: it marks where the market stops.

Section 08 · Two ways to price it

Two ways to price it — and why the number is not final until we have walked through.

Both columns assume a launch within a week of the walkthrough, with new photography, floor plans and the ad campaign ready on day one. The range in Section 06 is an educated estimate from the records; the strategy is finalized once we have seen the home.

The pocket's own history decides the approach. Both sales this year opened well above where they closed and gave back 8–15% of the original ask over three months; all four actives are doing the same thing now. Condominium buyers here compare the fee and the price side by side, and the listing that reads as the best value on both is the one that gets the showing.

What we do for your property

The campaign makes one argument, everywhere: the best value in the pocket on both numbers.

TH 43 has what the units it competes with do not — hardwood and stone, a third bath, a garden walk-out, a garage and a drive — at a lower price than the one in its own complex. The listing says that in the first line, the photographs prove it, and the ads put it in front of the first-time buyers and young families who are shopping condominium townhouses between $550,000 and $700,000 in south Scarborough right now.

Production

  • Professional photography — new photographs — the 2019 set is seven years old — staged and lit to show the floors and the west light
  • Videography and aerial drone — the enclave and its setting back from Kingston Road; a walkthrough that sells the multi-level layout
  • Floor plans — every level measured and drafted — the plan is the thing a multi-level buyer cannot picture from photographs
  • The comparison sheet — TH 43 beside HS47 and the Rockwood units — size, baths, fee, price — in every buyer's hand

Exposure

  • MLS® and full syndication — REALTOR.ca and every major portal, day one
  • Paid digital advertising, 24/7 — across our six pages for the life of the listing, aimed at first-time buyers and families in Scarborough and the east end
  • Collaborator posts — the tour reel on all six team pages at once, then to the large pages we work with
  • Agent network — a personal call to every agent who has sold a condominium townhouse in E08 this year
  • Database — featured to 30,000 contacts, including the first-time buyers moving up from condominium apartments

On the ground

  • Painting and touch-ups — where the walkthrough says they will return more than they cost
  • Staging — light staging of the main level and primary bedroom around your furniture
  • In-house legal review — the status certificate on the conditional offer, the conditions and the closing — checked before you sign
  • Showing protocol — agent-accompanied on your schedule; feedback to you within a day of every visit

Questions sellers ask

The things most people want to ask, answered before you have to.

Why not list higher and come down if we have to?

Because this pocket has already run that experiment four times this year. #14 in your complex opened at $831,000 and sold at $645,000 after four months; 3430 Kingston opened at $699,000 and sold at $550,000; HS47 has been coming down from $778,000 since April 2025 and is still for sale. Buyers here compare the fee and the price side by side and wait. The price the evidence supports on day one is the shortest route to the best number.

We paid $520,000 in 2019. Is that where the market has gone?

Roughly, yes. Toronto condominium townhouse prices are up about 11% since early 2019 after falling back from their 2022 peak, which carries $520,000 to about $577,000 — within a few thousand dollars of the midpoint built from the sales. The home has held its value through a market that gave back a great deal; it has not run ahead of it.

Does the $600 fee hurt us?

It is inside the pocket's range — $470 at Rockwood, $541 and $554 for the other two units in your complex, $635 at 3430 Kingston — and it includes water, insurance and parking. It is not a problem; it is a number every buyer will check, so the listing states it plainly and sets it beside what it covers. Worth confirming from the latest statement before we publish it.

Should we renovate the kitchen or baths before selling?

No. The most renovated unit in the complex — $200,000 of work — sold for $645,000 in August. A renovation would not return its cost, and it would cost you the weeks. Paint, touch-ups and staging where the walkthrough says they return more than they cost is the line.

What is a status certificate and when does it get ordered?

A package from the corporation — its financials, reserve fund, insurance, rules and any legal matters — that a buyer's lawyer reviews before an offer firms up. We order it when a conditional offer is accepted, which keeps the cost off your side until there is a buyer, and our in-house review reads it before the buyer's lawyer does. There are no known issues with YCC 392.

Is there tax on the sale?

A home you have lived in as your principal residence is generally exempt from tax on the gain. The exception worth a question is any period it was rented out. Terrence is a CPA and will make sure the right question is asked before the listing goes live.

How long will it take?

The pocket's two sales took 87 and 110 days — but both started well above the market and spent most of that time coming down to it. Priced at the evidence, with new photography and the comparison with HS47 and Rockwood working for you, 30 to 45 days to an offer is the reasonable expectation, with a 30–60 day close after that.

Who will we actually be dealing with?

Heaven and Terrence, on every call, showing and offer. The team is behind the file — a Broker for the contract, a law-trained partner for the status certificate and the agreement — but the two people accountable to you are the two whose names are on this document.
